reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / standard immunology references
clinicalPearls: APECED is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by mutations in the AIRE gene, which governs central immune tolerance in the thymus
It is classically defined by a triad of chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis, hypoparathyroidism, and primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison disease), with diagnosis usually requiring two of the three
Chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis is often the earliest feature and is driven by autoantibodies against Th17-related cytokines (such as IL-17 and IL-22)
The candidiasis reflects immune dysregulation rather than a classical phagocyte or T-cell deficiency, and is largely limited to skin, nails, and mucosa without systemic dissemination
A wide range of additional autoimmune conditions can occur, including gonadal failure, type 1 diabetes, autoimmune thyroid disease, hepatitis, pernicious anaemia, and vitiligo
A useful diagnostic marker is the presence of high-titre autoantibodies against type 1 interferons, which are highly characteristic of the condition
Chronic oral candidiasis carries a long-term risk of oral squamous cell carcinoma, warranting surveillance
Management involves hormone replacement for the endocrine deficiencies, antifungal treatment for candidiasis, and monitoring for the emergence of new autoimmune components over time
reference.pathophysiology: APECED results from biallelic mutations in AIRE (the autoimmune regulator), a transcriptional regulator expressed by medullary thymic epithelial cells that drives the display of tissue-specific self antigens during T-cell development. Defective AIRE function impairs negative selection, allowing autoreactive T cells to escape into the periphery and mount organ-specific autoimmune attacks. The result is progressive autoimmune destruction of endocrine and other tissues. The characteristic mucocutaneous candidiasis is explained by the generation of neutralising autoantibodies against Th17 cytokines that are essential for mucosal antifungal defence, and neutralising autoantibodies against type 1 interferons serve as a highly specific biomarker.
additionalDifferentials: Autoimmune polyendocrine syndrome type 2 (polygenic, adult onset)
Isolated chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis due to other genetic causes (for example STAT1 gain-of-function)
Other combined causes of endocrine autoimmunity
additionalInvestigations: Autoantibodies against type 1 interferons and against Th17 cytokines
Organ-specific autoantibody panels and endocrine function tests (calcium, parathyroid hormone, adrenal axis, thyroid, glucose)
Fungal cultures and clinical assessment of mucocutaneous candidiasis
Periodic screening for evolving autoimmune components
Surveillance for oral squamous cell carcinoma in chronic oral candidiasis
redFlags: Adrenal crisis from unrecognised or undertreated primary adrenal insufficiency requiring emergency treatment
New oral lesions raising concern for squamous cell carcinoma
Autoimmune hepatitis progressing to liver failure
Emergence of a new autoimmune endocrinopathy needing prompt recognition
reference.prognosis: With appropriate hormone replacement and antifungal therapy the prognosis is generally reasonable, but outcome is shaped by the cumulative burden of autoimmune organ damage, the risk of unrecognised adrenal crisis, and the long-term risk of oral malignancy, so lifelong monitoring is required.
pitfalls: Treating individual endocrinopathies in isolation without recognising the unifying syndrome
Missing evolving components, since the full picture develops over years
Overlooking adrenal insufficiency, with the danger of a precipitated crisis
Failing to survey chronic oral candidiasis for malignant change
Confusing APECED with IPEX, which is X-linked, FOXP3-related, and presents in infancy
management: Replace failing endocrine axes: glucocorticoid and mineralocorticoid for adrenal insufficiency, calcium with an activated vitamin D analogue (alfacalcidol or calcitriol) for hypoparathyroidism, levothyroxine for hypothyroidism, insulin for type 1 diabetes, and sex-hormone replacement for gonadal failure
Treat chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis with azole antifungals such as fluconazole, cycling agents to manage emerging azole resistance
Prevent and treat adrenal crisis with parenteral hydrocortisone and fluids, plus patient stress-dosing education, an emergency steroid card and an injection kit
Manage other autoimmune components as they arise, for example immunosuppression for autoimmune hepatitis and vitamin B12 replacement for pernicious anaemia
Undertake lifelong periodic screening for evolving endocrine and organ-specific autoimmunity, and surveillance for oral squamous cell carcinoma in chronic candidiasis
Coordinate care through endocrinology, clinical immunology and dermatology
Offer genetic counselling for this autosomal recessive AIRE disorder and screen affected siblings
